Based on revelations from the security experts as Kaspersky Labs, Reuters sources claim the NSA is placing spyware within drives from the likes of Western Digital, Seagate and Toshiba.
I think it's possible for encryption to still offer some protection at this level.

To what degree of 'possible' and what level is 'some'? If a device is rooted, or a BIOS or firmware is compromised, or any exploit sits at a 'low' layer, it is my understanding that every layer above the exploited layer is then considered compromised. Encryption that most people use (TrueCrypt, LUKS, BitLocker, etc) sits on top of the hardware firmware, BIOS and OS. If any layer is compromised underneath that encryption program, your passwords would theoretically be able to be sniffed, ie like a key logger. Moreover, once your encrypted data is decrypted so you can actually use it, the decrypted stream would then be readable by the exploit. In this regard, I believe the use of key files would be considered compromised as well.

Edit: Off the top of my head, I'm not sure how this would affect biometric-based or RSA-based two-factor authentication, but I don't see why it wouldn't be similarly affected.

My question is, what hardware is trusted anymore? What is a manufacturer from whom I can buy my hardware without having to fear it being backdoored or otherwise compromised? Chinese hardware doesn't feel any more safer.
